dialogue.shona: Zvifambiso zvinotakura vanhu zvakamira pachiteshi. Zvakanyorwa zvakasiyana-siyana kukwezva vafambi.
dialogue.english: Things fambiso things notakura people zvakamira on / at chiteshi zvakanyorwa zvakasiyana-siyana to / at kwezva people fambi.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakamira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakamira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('zvinotakura')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvinotakura' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'Zvakanyorwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'Zvakanyorwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.

cultural_notes.title: Shona Cultural & Everyday Context (Lesson 1)
cultural_notes.content: This expression ('Zvifambiso zvinotakura vanhu zvakamira pachiteshi. Zvakanyorwa zvakasiyana-siyana kukwezva vafambi.' — "Things fambiso things notakura people zvakamira on / at chiteshi zvakanyorwa zvakasiyana-siyana to / at kwezva people fambi.") reflects how Shona speakers connect daily family life, work, and community relationships across urban towns and rural homesteads ('kumusha') in Zimbabwe.

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?
Translate this new sentence into English: 'Tora mvura uinwe.'
options: Take the water and drink it.
Put the cup on the table before you leave.
Close the window because it is cold outside.
Come here and help me carry the books.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Take the water and drink it.

active_exercises.prompt: If someone says 'Ndinonzwa nyota, ndinoda kunwa mukaka kana mvura', what are they asking for?
options: Bread and sugar because it is morning
Milk or water because they feel thirsty
Maize meal and cooking oil from the market
Salt and vegetables for the evening meal
active_exercises.correct_answer: Milk or water because they feel thirsty
